claims.text: A homogeneous, nanostructured high-entropy-alloy microstructure enables rapid formation of a passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film formed on the high-entropy alloy is mechanically robust and self-healing.
Microstructural and chemical homogeneity minimizes local galvanic effects.
A homogenized, thermomechanically processed CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy can have a uniform, fine-grained microstructure and a native oxide layer.
A uniform nanoscale grain structure results in a continuous, adherent passive oxide film across grains and grain boundaries.
Sliding contact periodically removes the passive film during tribocorrosion.
High configurational entropy and a homogeneous alloy structure facilitate rapid reformation of the removed film through oxidation.
Rapid passive-film reformation establishes a dynamic removal–reformation equilibrium.
The proposed dynamic equilibrium reduces localized corrosion by limiting chemical inhomogeneity.
The proposed dynamic equilibrium limits material loss caused by wear–corrosion synergy.
Compared with a compositionally similar but less homogeneous or lower-entropy baseline, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit lower combined degradation.
The high-entropy alloy will have lower wear volume than the baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will have lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
The improvement will be most observable under moderate mechanical loads and corrosion potentials that permit repassivation.
The prediction should hold when film reformation can keep pace with mechanically induced film removal.
The mechanism may fail at extreme loads, very high temperatures, or extremely low pH because film removal can exceed the reformation rate.
The mechanism may fail if high configurational entropy does not sufficiently suppress galvanic coupling.
Passive-film reformation kinetics and degradation improvements are sensitive to electrolyte composition, mechanical load, and temperature.
